items.question: Why do you think AI systems should develop hypotheses through a process of compositional refinement?
items.object: Compositional programs and hypothesis refinement
items.answer: I think it's kind of true and obviously true that programs—programming languages—are compositional, right? We build more and more complex programs by understanding the parts and then combining them together to build more and more complex parts. Most of the hypothesis development that we do as humans is of this form, both as an individual and as science as a whole, right? Science as a whole collectively finds hypotheses, and then we revise them communally in conferences like this. So it seems natural to me to say that we should build systems that have this kind of refinement process. One of the hard things in trying to mechanize this is: how do you guide or reinforce good refinement paths?

The response identifies guiding or reinforcing productive hypothesis-refinement paths as a challenge in mechanizing hypothesis development.

items.question: What do you think the current discourse on AI world models overlooks?
items.object: World models at multiple levels of abstraction
items.answer: Another axis that I think is important—you know, Kevin said this—is this kind of tall tower of abstractions. A key thing somewhat overlooked in the current discourse on world models is that there isn't a single world model, right? You can understand things at multiple different levels. There's multiple different models. You can build pretty much anything, right? There's a camera right here. I've got a model of how this camera works at the level of: I press this button and an image is taken. But I can also understand the internal structure, like the wires and the circuits, or I can go down to the sensor in the camera. All of these are different models that are useful for different things that you need to do with that model.

items.question: How would you like the principles of everyday science to shape the way AI systems learn?
items.object: Everyday science as a foundation for AI learning
items.answer: We want to avoid building these Frankenstein systems where we are hard-coding a whole bunch of different knowledge representation and heuristics. But in those cases, as you're alluding to, it required smart people to look at the world and say, “Okay, here are the inductive biases. Let me encode these into the system.” We think the principles underlying everyday science—how do we form hypotheses, how do we revise those beliefs, how do we take actions to learn about how the world works—are the same principles in everyday science that apply to real science. We want systems that can do that, that can learn how to interact with new toys and devices and interfaces in a way which isn't large-scale imitation learning, right?

items.question: How do you think about scaling as a strategy for building intelligence?
items.object: Scaling as a strategy for building intelligence
items.answer: I think there's a lot of good lessons from this scaling round. We do actually want algorithms which can make use of the new hardware that we have. At the same time, it's not the full story. I think our personal belief is that that's not going to carry us all the way. And also pragmatically, there are other people clearly trying to carry that torch. If it does get us all the way, then maybe we should hedge and do things that draw on the amazing GPUs and amazing pre-trained models we have, but which also bring to bear ideas from cognitive science, classic AI, and so on.

items.question: How do you view the Bayesian paradigm as an explanation of how humans learn from examples?
items.object: The Bayesian paradigm of learning from examples
items.answer: I think there's many possible answers to that. I do somewhat believe in the Bayesian paradigm, which is that you have beliefs about how the world works. When you observe examples, you incorporate that knowledge into your current hypothesis about how the world works. But that's a very abstract theory. The question is how that was actually implemented. The reality is it's probably approximate. We're probably not doing exact Bayesian inference. So there's a nice foundation to think about how an ideal agent should incorporate knowledge, and then there are practical questions about how to build systems that do that.

items.question: What does building intelligent machines from first principles mean to you in the context of current mainstream machine learning?
items.object: Building intelligent machines from first principles
items.answer: As Kevin said, we're very much not anti-large-scale deep machine learning. We're building these tools. We're using these tools. I would say the main distinction between how I think of the work that we do and what we want to do is: can we build things from first principles? A lot of current mainstream machine learning is basically large-scale imitation learning. That's because it's so effective, and it's producing all of these amazing tools. But both from a scientific perspective and from an engineering perspective, can we understand some of the principles about how to build intelligent machines from the ground up? I think there are some of the pieces: uncertainty, causality, reasoning in general. But there are many things that we don't know. Part of having a research program is trying to figure out those missing parts.

items.question: How do you distinguish the compositionality of programming languages from that of natural language?
items.object: Programming languages as compositional languages
items.answer: One of the, in my view, most interesting examples of compositional languages are just programming languages, right? I think it's obviously true that programming languages are compositional. We build more and more complex programs by understanding the parts and then combining them together. One of the differences between programming languages and natural language is that programming languages are strictly compositional, whereas in natural language there are all these heuristics, phrases where you have to just learn the thing.

items.question: How do you think about the different approaches to building AI systems that generate programs and other compositional structures?
items.object: Methods for generating programs and compositional structures
items.answer: There are many ways. A lot of old-fashioned ways start with a grammar, expand that grammar, search through it, and try and find a program by searching a grammar space. Now people are using language models to generate programs and compositional structures. There's an interesting spectrum of approaches where there's a question of how much semantic knowledge about the compositional structure you incorporate into your model versus it being purely data-driven from examples. We've both worked on both and continue to work on both. But as Kevin said, the challenges are that if you've got a compositional structure, it's often of unbounded dimension, a very hard space to search through. You need smart methods to try and find the structure or the program within this vast space.

items.question: How do you think about comparing neural and symbolic approaches to solving problems such as ARC?
items.object: Comparing neural and symbolic approaches to solving ARC problems
items.answer: A neural network, or a particular neural network architecture, implements some algorithm. You can implement an algorithm in Python. The Bayesian paradigm is a normative model. It says what an ideal system should do, given essentially no consideration of compute. You could also ask what an ideal system would do if you had bounds on compute, or if you had to reason about how much compute you should use. I don't think of it necessarily as bottom up versus top down on this axis. You can think about composite methods which combine different kinds of systems. The paper that Kevin started and that we joined forces to work on and complete uses a combination of different methods. Kevin will talk more, I'm sure, but we have an induction and a transduction model. The induction model is a program in the case of ARC: a program that transforms the input to the output, like a Python program. The transduction model directly outputs the output grid given the input. I think it's important to consider different axes. One is the representation of the function: is it a Python program or a neural network? The other is the type signature of the thing that you're finding: are you directly outputting the final solution, or are you outputting a function which you can then apply to the input? We've explored a little bit of this grid of possibilities, but there's more we could think about.

items.question: How do you see programming languages evolving as AI becomes part of their design?
items.object: The evolution of programming languages
items.answer: I think it's really important to recognize that there's an evolution of programming languages. Kevin said this at the start: the original programming languages were basically long streams of instructions. Then we built in more and more forms of structure. There was a whole structured programming movement. Then we have a variety of different families of languages that we use in modern software engineering today: mainstream languages like Python, maybe slightly less mainstream languages but popular in other circles like Haskell and functional languages. The key thing for me is that beyond expressing computation, which is not that hard to do, we can express computation in many different systems. We've started to build more kinds of systems to help us build better programs: class structures, type structures, different modular structures. They allow us to encode more about the world within our programming languages and make them more useful. If you think of this as an evolution, as Kevin said, we've got to a point where they're pretty good, but there's room for development. We probably wouldn't expect that in 100 years everything will look exactly as things are now. An interesting question is how we expect the evolution of programming languages to develop. When you add AI in general into the picture, it becomes a lot harder to predict. Now we're seeing interesting compositions of ChatGPT calling out to Python and Python calling out to ChatGPT. It seems to be a moment of flux in the design space, and for me it's interesting to see how this will evolve over time.

items.question: How do you think about when building a reusable library is worthwhile?
items.object: Building reusable libraries as cached computation for current and future use
items.answer: One way to think about it is: as a programmer, why ever build a library function? There are a few different reasons. One, having a function can allow you to express your current program more compactly. I've got some shared structure, and I can reuse that in a variety of different ways within my current task. Another related reason is more future-looking. People build libraries not for their current program, but in the expectation that they or other people are going to use that functionality in the future. So I think you might be able to think about and perhaps even formalize when and why you want a library. It's something like: in the expectation of current and future uses, it's going to make my life easier. I'm going to be able to use this thing that I'm caching now, perhaps sometime in the future. We do this informally as software engineers. We build things that we think other people will eventually use. I think the mind probably does something like that in a very hand-wavy way. We're building structures that we expect we're going to be able to use and that we'd like to use sometime in the future. We have this cached computation that we can reuse at a future point. That's broadly how I would think of it, and you can perhaps even try and formalize and cash that out in some kind of rational decision theory.

items.question: How do you distinguish the mental experiments you perform when solving ARC from interaction with real-world systems?
items.object: ARC and interaction over time
items.answer: I intuitively feel when I'm solving ARC, I'm doing little mental experiments to try and look at that test and perform this hypothesis. But the actual domain itself doesn't require me to take any sequence of actions. In contrast, most things in the real world are not like that. Most things in the real world require you to interact with the system through time. The canonical example is games. If I'm playing some video game, I'm taking a sequence of actions to try and explore that.

items.question: How do you understand the Autumn project's attempt to infer a video game's source code as a form of science?
items.object: Autumn's synthesis of world models and hidden state
items.answer: The goal there was to build a system that could synthesize essentially the source code of a video game after observing interactions with that video game. The background proposition is that doing so is a kind of science. If you can observe some dynamics and infer the source code of the underlying world behind the dynamics, that's something like understanding. That's something like building a model of how that world works. The paper we did was to build a little DSL for a certain class of interactive games, if you will. The way in which they're not games is that there's no external reward function. It's just an environment which a system can interact with. From traces provided by humans of these games or environments, the autumn synthesis method infers the underlying code. One of the key things we wanted to explore there was what you might call latent state: things that are true about the world but you can't directly observe. The real world is full of things like this. Pretty much everything has some hidden state that we can't observe, and this hidden state is often very complicated and dynamic. It's probably best described by some kind of program evolving over time. A key contribution there is asking whether we can infer this hidden latent state in addition to the entire full program.

items.question: What do you see as the central limitation of the models inferred by Autumn?
items.object: Abstraction as a limitation and future direction for Autumn
items.answer: In that work the programs or models that we inferred are not abstract. They're ground-truth models of the world, and we don't really think this is how human thinking works or even could work. There has to be some abstraction. There have to be some parts of reality that we omit or discard from our models. A big open question is how can you infer abstract models? How can you infer models that omit the right parts of the world in order to be practical and useful? We didn't really explore that within autumn, but this is very high on our minds of things that we want to explore, and on the minds of others in the community too.

items.question: Why do you find resource rationality compelling as a way to choose the right abstraction?
items.object: Resource rationality as a framework for choosing abstractions
items.answer: Maybe the framework that I find quite compelling is resource rationality. This is basically saying that you should try to do the best you can with the resources that you can. It's a slightly convoluted statement, but the idea is that you have some kind of belief, some distribution over possible tasks or uses of a model. You have computational constraints; you can't run things forever. A way you can cash out this question of when you should choose the right abstraction, or what kind of abstraction you should construct, is to say: I've got some beliefs about how I'm going to use this model. It needs to allow me to answer the task and incur computational costs, so I should consider all of those things and do the optimal thing.

items.question: What do you want a poly-structural representation of world models to capture?
items.object: Poly-structural representations of world models
items.answer: Another axis I think is important—Kevin said this—is the tower of abstractions. A key thing somewhat overlooked in the current discourse on world models is that there isn't a single world model. You can understand things at multiple different levels. There are multiple different models. You can build pretty much anything. There's a camera right here. I've got a model of how this camera works at the level of: I press this button and an image is taken. I can also understand the internal structure, like the wires and circuits, or go down to the sensor in the camera. All of these are different models that are useful for different things that you need to do with that model. There's no single correct answer except physics. A key goal for us is to embrace that plurality and try and find representations of models which incorporate a plurality of different models within them. I've been using the term poly-structural to capture this idea. We'll see if that term sticks. Whatever you call it, we need to encode multiple different models of reality and the relationship between those models. As a human modeler, let's say a formal scientific modeler, if I'm modeling Covid, I can say hair color doesn't matter in my Covid model. But this relationship between the model and reality is encoded in my head as the scientist. We want that relationship to be within the computational formalism itself. In my sense, that's a hard scientific computer science question which I think hasn't fully been explored. Maybe it will just emerge from scale and data. I don't know; it's a question of whether we have to build these things in or whether they'll emerge.

items.question: What role do you see for learned neural networks in automating the discovery of useful abstractions?
items.object: Learned neural networks in automated abstraction discovery
items.answer: We want to avoid building Frankenstein systems where we are hard-coding a whole bunch of different knowledge representations and heuristics for reasoning with those representations. Instead, we want something which looks more like rational analysis from first principles. When you do that, you immediately run into hard computational problems. You get a big search space; it might even be harder in the inner loop to evaluate how good a model or abstraction is, because you need to retrospectively say whether this would be good for the kinds of reasoning tasks I expect. That computational problem is a place where I think it'd be good to insert learned neural networks that have good intuitions about everyday common-sense abstractions and can propose them. They can say this code would probably be valuable in this situation. items.question: How do you think Bayesian models of cognition should acquire their inductive biases?
items.object: Learning implicit inductive biases for Bayesian models of cognition
items.answer: If you look at the history of Bayesian computational models of cognition, a lot of which was done by psychologists and cognitive scientists like Josh Tenenbaum and others, there's a really compelling and strong history of expressing some prior knowledge and showing that humans do something like approximate posterior Bayesian inference conditional on the data. But often in those cases, it required smart people to look at the world and say, “Okay, here are the inductive biases. Let me encode these into the system.” I think the bitter lesson of AI is that when you can, you shouldn't encode explicit inductive biases; this will lose out relative to learning these from the data if you've got lots and lots of data and lots and lots of compute. In my mind, there's something obviously right about the fact that you need priors and you can incorporate data to revise your beliefs. Again, I think Bayesian theory is a good normative theory for that. But that doesn't mean you have to adhere to the classical tradition of explicitly encoding these inductive biases. I think there's a potential paradigm of saying, “Let's encode priors, but let's try and learn these as implicitly as possible.” Where do you learn these from? It could be the standard paradigm in modern machine learning, where you're learning these biases from large corpuses of data. They could be richer corpuses than just internet data. There are all the things that you do as a human. I can observe you and infer some of your beliefs. You could imagine richer sources of data than just internet data that would allow us to get closer to the inductive biases that humans have. It's tricky to actually implement these systems. You face hard computational problems. But broadly speaking, doing inductive inference over large corpuses of data to learn implicit inductive biases, as opposed to explicit hand-coded ones, is a promising path to pursue.

items.question: How do you understand the convergence of connectionist and symbolic approaches to AI?
items.object: The convergence of connectionist and symbolic approaches to AI
items.answer: There's something obviously right about scale, and there's something obviously right about learning. A connectionist architecture allows you to learn from large amounts of data. There's also something obviously right about symbolic architectures, in the sense that most of our modern society is built on top of them. I think there's also something right about general normative principles of intelligence. Given that, the question is: what should you do? Can you take the things that we know to be right and compose them in a way that makes sense? I think you're seeing that in a variety of ways. From the large labs, like OpenAI, they have large models trained on huge amounts of data. But they have these scaffolds around them, where the models call out to Python to do some computation. Why is that a smart thing to do? Because Python's an effective language for a certain class of computations, much more effective than a neural network for a large class of things. They've come to a business decision that it's useful to have this kind of hybrid system. From the other perspective, there's a history of symbolic systems, and from a different perspective I've realized that you can't model the entire world through a list of propositional formulae. The real world is a lot messier and more complex than that. We want to do nice reasoning, but we have to handle the complexity of reality. This immediately leads to architectures which can do both of these things. Both the complexity of the world and what we want from reasoning and learning systems are leading to a convergence of ideas right now. I think that convergence is composition: taking these systems and plugging them together. The real question is, can we do better than that? Can we go from the ground up and re-engineer systems that have the functional things that we want, but may not look architecturally like the systems that we have today?

items.question: Why do you see everyday science as a useful focus for Project MARA's effort to build systems that learn through interaction?
items.object: Everyday science as a focus of Project MARA
items.answer: Within this high-level goal of building what you might call a general MARA system, a system where you can plug it into the world and it takes actions to learn about that world and build an internal model, we're focused on a narrower subset, which is what we call everyday science. We've discussed this today in various contexts. There's real science, what we do as chemists and biologists and computer scientists, learning about the physical and artificial world. But then there's also everyday science, what we do as normal humans, adults and children. We learn about a new AC system in my hotel, or a new microwave, or a new toy. We think the principles underlying this everyday science—how do we form hypotheses, how do we revise those beliefs, how do we take actions to learn about how the world works—are the same principles in everyday science that apply to real science. We want systems that can do that, that can learn how to interact with new toys and devices and interfaces in a way which isn't large-scale imitation learning. As part of a real approach to AI, to science, even if it's not actually discovering new useful science.
